explanations.explanation: Elihu, the young man speaking to Job, says it plainly: "For the ear tests words as the mouth tastes food." (Job 34:3) So you don't just swallow every word that comes by. You check it first. I never send out a batch without sampling the dough, and Elihu wants the same care with words.
Singing is a nice picture, but it isn't the one Elihu uses. He's talking about testing, not praising. The mouth in his comparison is busy tasting, and the ear is busy checking what it hears.

I'm a story fan, so I get the pull, baker. But Elihu's comparison isn't about telling anything. He says the ear tests words the way the mouth tastes food (Job 34:3), so it's about checking what comes in.

Not quite, friend. Elihu says, "Let us choose for ourselves what is right; let us learn together what is good." (Job 34:4) Notice the word "together." He's inviting the wise men to sort it out with him, not leaving them alone to do it.

Right, baker. Elihu says, "Let us choose for ourselves what is right; let us learn together what is good." (Job 34:4) He puts himself in the group with the word "us." Nobody gets sent off to figure it out solo.

explanations.answer: He is righteous but God denied him justice
explanations.explanation: That's it. Elihu quotes Job as saying, "I am righteous, yet God has deprived me of justice." (Job 34:5) Keep in mind this is Elihu reporting Job's words, and Elihu is about to push back on them. Job is the one who lost his children, his wealth and his health, so you can see where that feeling is coming from.

explanations.answer: He sinned and earned all his suffering
explanations.explanation: That's actually the opposite of what Elihu quotes. He has Job saying, "I am righteous." (Job 34:5) So Job isn't owning up to a list of sins in this line. He's saying God has deprived him of justice.

explanations.answer: His friends are the ones who wronged him
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think that, since Job has had plenty of people talking at him. But in this verse the complaint Elihu quotes is aimed at God: "God has deprived me of justice." (Job 34:5) Job's friends aren't the ones named here.
Yes, baker. Elihu says Job "keeps company with evildoers and walks with wicked men." (Job 34:8) That's a hard thing to say about a man. Elihu says it, and the text leaves it right there.

Kings and nobles do show up later in this speech, but not as Job's company. Elihu brings them up when he talks about what God says to them (Job 34:18). Here in verse 8, the company Job keeps is evildoers and wicked men.
The poor and the afflicted do come up in this speech, friend. Their cry comes before God in verse 28. But in verse 8, Elihu says Job keeps company with evildoers and walks with wicked men.
Right. Elihu says Job has said, "It profits a man nothing that he should delight in God." (Job 34:9) That's Elihu's report of what Job said. The thing Elihu says gets no profit is delighting in God.
Wisdom is a good thing to delight in, baker, but it isn't what this verse says. Elihu quotes Job as saying it profits a man nothing to delight in God (Job 34:9). The word that fills the blank is God.

Nope, riches don't come into this verse at all. The thing Elihu says Job claims has no profit is delighting in God (Job 34:9). I've sold plenty of cookies, but nobody ever tried to say they were profit-free.

That's the one. "Far be it from God to do wrong, and from the Almighty to act unjustly." (Job 34:10) Elihu has been warming up, and this is his big claim. He's saying God doing wrong is about as far away as it gets.
Elihu doesn't say that here, friend. What he says is far from God and the Almighty is doing wrong and acting unjustly (Job 34:10). Mercy isn't the topic of this verse.
Dreams don't show up in this verse, baker. Elihu says, "Far be it from God to do wrong, and from the Almighty to act unjustly." (Job 34:10) That's the thing he says is far from God.
Yes. Elihu says, "according to a man's deeds He repays him." (Job 34:11) He follows it up with, "according to a man's ways He brings consequences." So deeds and ways are what he points to.
Wealth isn't what Elihu names. He says God repays a man "according to a man's deeds" (Job 34:11). Deeds are what go into that repayment.

Good guess, since prayer matters in plenty of places. But in this verse, Elihu says God repays "according to a man's deeds" and brings consequences "according to a man's ways." (Job 34:11) Prayers aren't mentioned.

Yes, baker. Elihu says that if God were to set His heart to it and withdraw His Spirit and breath, "all flesh would perish together and mankind would return to the dust." (Job 34:14-15) He's making a point that all life depends on God. And he asks who gave God charge over the earth to begin with.

It's true, friend. Elihu says that if God withdrew His Spirit and breath, "all flesh would perish together and mankind would return to the dust." (Job 34:14-15) He says it to show how much rests in God's hands. So this one is a plain yes.

That's not what Elihu says, friend. He describes God as the One "who says to kings, 'You are worthless!' and to nobles, 'You are wicked.'" (Job 34:18) Not much going easy in that sentence. Kings get no special treatment.

Right. Elihu describes the One "who says to kings, 'You are worthless!' and to nobles, 'You are wicked.'" (Job 34:18) Then he adds that God is not partial to princes (Job 34:19). Titles don't buy anybody a gentler word.

explanations.answer: They are all the work of His hands
explanations.explanation: That's what he says, baker. God "does not favor rich over poor" and the reason Elihu gives is, "For they are all the work of His hands." (Job 34:19) Princes and poor are made by the same hands. That's why nobody gets favorites.

explanations.answer: The poor pray more often than the rich
explanations.explanation: Elihu doesn't say anything about who prays more, friend. His reason is, "For they are all the work of His hands." (Job 34:19) It's about who made them, not what they do.

explanations.answer: The poor have suffered far more
explanations.explanation: That might sound fair to some, but it's not what Elihu says. He gives one reason: "For they are all the work of His hands." (Job 34:19) Suffering isn't the reason in this verse.

Elihu says the opposite, baker. "There is no darkness or deep shadow where the workers of iniquity can hide." (Job 34:22) The verse before it says God's eyes are on the ways of a man and that He sees his every step. I've hidden in a pantry once, and even that didn't work.
Right. Elihu says, "There is no darkness or deep shadow where the workers of iniquity can hide." (Job 34:22) He's saying no shadow is deep enough. Not even the middle of the night.

explanations.answer: Sets up others in their place
explanations.explanation: That's it. Elihu says God "shatters the mighty without inquiry and sets up others in their place." (Job 34:24) So the seats don't stay empty. Someone else gets set there.
Not quite, baker. Elihu says God "sets up others in their place." (Job 34:24) So the place gets filled. Somebody else is set up there.

explanations.answer: Hands their power to the poor
explanations.explanation: Elihu doesn't say that here, friend. He says God "sets up others in their place." (Job 34:24) The verse says "others" and doesn't say who they are.

Yes. Elihu says God strikes them "because they turned aside from Him and had no regard for any of His ways." (Job 34:27) That's the reason he gives. Turning aside from Him and not caring about His ways.
Offerings aren't what Elihu names, baker. His reason is that "they turned aside from Him and had no regard for any of His ways." (Job 34:27) Nothing in this verse is about skipped offerings.

explanations.answer: They grew too rich and proud
explanations.explanation: That might seem like a natural reason, but Elihu doesn't say it. He says they "turned aside from Him and had no regard for any of His ways." (Job 34:27) Riches and pride aren't named in this verse.
Right, baker. Elihu says, "They caused the cry of the poor to come before Him, and He heard the outcry of the afflicted." (Job 34:28) So the cry reached God, and He heard it.
Not the rich, friend. Elihu says they "caused the cry of the poor to come before Him." (Job 34:28) And he adds that God heard the outcry of the afflicted.
Nobles show up earlier in this speech, in verse 18, but not here. In verse 28, Elihu says they "caused the cry of the poor to come before Him." The word that fits is poor.
Yes, baker. Elihu says, "Yet He watches over both man and nation." (Job 34:29) He says it right after the questions about God staying silent and hiding His face. So even then, the watching goes on.

explanations.answer: Rests from all of His work
explanations.explanation: Elihu doesn't say that, friend. The line is, "Yet He watches over both man and nation." (Job 34:29) Watching is what he says God keeps doing.

explanations.answer: Leaves the world to its kings
explanations.explanation: That's not what Elihu says. He says God "watches over both man and nation." (Job 34:29) And in the next verse, he says it's so that godless men should not rule (Job 34:30).

That's right, baker. Elihu says God watches over man and nation, "that godless men should not rule or lay snares for the people." (Job 34:29-30) So the watching has a purpose attached to it in his words. He's saying godless men shouldn't rule.

It's true, friend. Elihu says God "watches over both man and nation, that godless men should not rule or lay snares for the people." (Job 34:29-30) That's what the verse says. So the answer is a plain yes.
Not quite, baker. Elihu says, "You must choose, not I; so tell me what you know." (Job 34:33) He hands the choosing over and then asks for what Job knows. Elihu isn't the one making this choice.
Right. Elihu says, "You must choose, not I; so tell me what you know." (Job 34:33) The choice isn't his. He turns it back and asks what Job knows.

That's the line. Elihu says the wise men will declare, "Job speaks without knowledge; his words lack insight." (Job 34:35) Keep in mind this is what Elihu says they will say. It's a hard thing to hear about a man who has lost so much.

explanations.answer: Job has been wronged by God
explanations.explanation: That's what Elihu quotes Job as saying earlier, in verse 5. In verse 35, what he says the wise men will say is, "Job speaks without knowledge; his words lack insight." Elihu isn't saying they'll agree with Job.

explanations.answer: Job is wiser than all of them
explanations.explanation: Elihu says the opposite, baker. He says the wise men will say, "Job speaks without knowledge; his words lack insight." (Job 34:35) Nobody gets crowned the wisest in that line.
Yes, baker. Elihu says Job "adds rebellion to his sin; he claps his hands among us and multiplies his words against God." (Job 34:37) That's how Elihu ends this speech. And the story isn't over yet.
I get why you'd think that, since Elihu is the one talking. But he says Job "multiplies his words against God." (Job 34:37) The blank is God.
Close, since Elihu does talk about men all through this speech. But in the last verse he says Job "multiplies his words against God." (Job 34:37) The blank is God.
